name: r3-external-2
statement: The RL-Zero-Math weight difference is the sum of two parts learned at different times: an early sharpening of the base's own solution distribution that turns problems the base solves only sometimes into problems it solves reliably, which the fully trained delta overshoots several-fold (as in ExPO, the optimal scale shrinks with training) and so is fully expressed at a ≈ 0.25; and a part from prolonged training that adds solutions where the base rarely succeeds (as in ProRL) and grows roughly in proportion to a. So partial deltas and orthogonal RL deltas recover most of the gap on MATH-500 but only a small share on hard328 and on problems no base sample solves.
scope: Covers base + a(RL - base) merges, the Code-RL delta and the full 3.1 RL-Zero-Math model against the cued Olmo-3-1025-7B base at T 1.0 / top-p 1.0, cap 16,384, grader v3, on MATH-500 and the clean hard328. It speaks to accuracy per difficulty class and to which problems are fixed or lost. It does not cover sampling-temperature effects or loops at T 0.6, nor answer-format effects of the plain prompt beyond noting that format is part of the early, saturating part. The early part is described by its effect (reliability on base-solvable problems), not located in particular weights.

imports.finding: Extrapolating a fine-tuning delta helps only within the first-order regime; the optimal extra scale shrinks as training goes on (8.0, 2.5, 0.5, 0.3 at 10-100 % of steps), and long training adds spurious features such as length bias, with too large a scale giving gibberish or non-termination.
imports.how: Explains why a quarter of the final delta already saturates the early sharpening part: by step 2,800 that part is overshot several-fold, so scaling it down costs nothing while extra scale (a > 1) adds only length and word-salad tails.

imports.finding: RL's pass@k gain is negatively correlated with the base's pass@k; tasks the base already handles plateau early with unchanged or narrowed boundaries, while hard tasks keep gaining at every k with prolonged training.
imports.how: Defines the second part: the gain on problems the base rarely solves comes from late training and is not saturated, so it shrinks roughly in proportion when the delta is scaled down and is missing from a delta trained on another domain (Code).

explains.quote: a=0.25 is +6.2 pts over base cue [3.0, 9.6], later steps flat
explains.how: The early sharpening part saturates by a = 0.25, and the late part is small on MATH-500.
Format and reliability are early, overshot parts, so 0.25 of the delta gives 181 of the 239 plain-prompt points.

explains.quote: most of the RL direction's gain is 24 fewer lost problems
explains.how: Sharpening makes the base reliable on problems it already solves sometimes, so the gain shows up as fewer lost problems.
At a = 0.25 tokens barely move from the base's while accuracy is two-thirds of the way to RL: the saturating part is reliability, not longer deliberation, whose length bias grows with a.

explains.quote: Code-RL: plain 390, cue 450 (-1.4 vs RL cue [-4.0, 1.0])
explains.how: Any RL run sharpens the base's own distribution, so an orthogonal Code delta matches Math-RL on MATH-500, where the sharpening part dominates.
On harder problems more of the gap is the late, ProRL-type part that sharpening cannot supply.

explains.quote: By RL-length quartile (82 each) base/RL right: 78/82, 52/67, 30/45, 4/12
explains.how: The gap concentrates where the base rarely succeeds, the late part's domain.
On hard problems RL expands what can be solved at all, as ProRL reports for tasks where the base struggles.

explains.quote: Harder sets: RL leads the cued base by 5-12 points
explains.how: The shorter-trained 3.0 delta has the early part (ties the cue on MATH-500) but less of the late part, so it still leads only on harder sets.

explains.quote: 76 % of the gain in the first 200 RL steps
explains.how: Published RL dynamics put the sharpening part early in training, so the final delta overshoots it.

conflicts.how: If the MATH-500 gain were only sharpening, pass@4 should nearly converge; a 15-problem pass@4 lead means some late, coverage-expanding gain on MATH-500 too.

An early sharpening part should already show some activation divergence at step 100; it is near the noise floor, so the early part must form between steps 100 and ~400 or be invisible to activation correlation.

rival: A one-dimensional reading: the delta moves a single competence variable, accuracy is a saturating function of a, and every difficulty class saturates at the same a, so a = 0.25 recovers about two-thirds of the gap everywhere and Code-RL matches Math-RL on any benchmark. The separating observation is theta(0.25) and Code-RL with the cue on hard328: the rival predicts roughly 164 + 0.66 x 41 ≈ 191 right of 328 for theta(0.25) and about 200 for Code-RL; this theory predicts only about a quarter of the hard328 gap (about 174) and a similarly small share for Code-RL, and on MATH-500 problems that two base samples both miss, theta(0.25) gains far less than RL does.

predictions.experiment: theta(0.25) = base + 0.25 (RL - base), bf16 stochastic rounding as in the existing merge cells, RL tokenizer, cue, clean hard328, one sample, T 1.0 / top-p 1.0, cap 16,384, seed base 3,000,000, grader v3.
predictions.refuted_by: 189 or more right of 328 (theta(0.25) recovers at least 60 % of the 42-problem hard328 gap, as on MATH-500).

predictions.experiment: allenai/Olmo-3.1-7B-RL-Zero-Code (1ca3bb30), RL-Math tokenizer, cue, clean hard328, one sample, T 1.0 / top-p 1.0, cap 16,384, seed base 3,000,000, grader v3.
predictions.refuted_by: 190 or more right of 328 (Code-RL closes most of the hard328 gap, as it does on MATH-500).

predictions.experiment: Offline: theta(0.25)'s success on MATH-500 problems that two independent base samples both miss.
predictions.recipe: Files: studies/rlneurons/results/rln4/t1_t2_items-01/per_problem.json (fields problem_index, t1_right), iterate-runs:abaybektursun-1114-153047-6429/answers.jsonl (random_cue; field score_v3) and iterate-runs:abaybektursun-1114-153102-b029/answers.jsonl (theta0.25_cue; field score_v3). Join the three on problem_index (500 problems; one row each). A row counts as right only if score_v3 is true (1); cap hits and missing answers count as wrong. H = problems with t1_right false AND random_cue score_v3 false. Statistic = (number of H problems with theta0.25_cue score_v3 true) / |H|.
predictions.refuted_by: A fraction of 0.42 or more (theta(0.25) recovers at least 80 % of the full RL model's rate of about 0.52 on these never-solved problems).

predictions.experiment: Offline: how many of the cued base's right MATH-500 problems theta(0.25) loses.
predictions.recipe: Files: studies/rlneurons/results/rln4/t1_t2_items-01/per_problem.json (problem_index, t1_right) and iterate-runs:abaybektursun-1114-153102-b029/answers.jsonl (theta0.25_cue, score_v3). Join on problem_index. Count problems with t1_right true and theta0.25_cue score_v3 not true (false, missing, or cap hit with no right answer).
predictions.refuted_by: 25 or more lost problems (theta(0.25) is no more reliable on base-solvable problems than the matched-norm random cell, which lost 35).

predictions.experiment: Offline: theta(0.25)'s success on MATH-500 problems the base solves sometimes (T1 wrong, fresh base sample right).
predictions.recipe: Same three files and join as the H recipe. S = problems with t1_right false AND random_cue score_v3 true. Statistic = (number of S problems with theta0.25_cue score_v3 true) / |S|; cap hits count as wrong.
predictions.refuted_by: A fraction below 0.6 (no sharpening gain on sometimes-solved problems beyond a fresh base sample).
